A close reading for the week

“Are there no prisons?”

A Christmas Carol · Stave One

Two visitors ask Scrooge to help people in immediate need. He answers with the names of institutions. Dickens lets the short questions reveal a whole habit of thought: distance, bookkeeping and a refusal to see poverty as a claim made by one person upon another.

“At this festive season of the year, Mr. Scrooge,” said the gentleman, taking up a pen, “it is more than usually desirable1 that we should make some slight provision for the Poor and destitute, who suffer greatly at the present time. Many thousands are in want of common necessaries; hundreds of thousands are in want of common comforts,2 sir.”

  1. 1

    The season sharpens the claim

    ‘Usually’ makes the poverty permanent; ‘more than’ makes winter and Christmas an extra weight. The appeal joins present suffering to a season that celebrates generosity.

  2. 2

    Not luxuries

    “Common” is repeated. Food, warmth and ordinary comfort are described as minimum needs shared by many, while the rising numbers make deprivation impossible to dismiss as a rare case.
